title: Report
text:
Code
library(tidyverse)
library(here)
library(haven)

allbus_mini_raw <-
  elect_clean <- read_csv(here("data", "processed", "elect_clean.csv"))
unemp <- read_csv(here("data", "processed", "unemp_clean.csv"))
allbus_mini_clean <- read_dta(here("data", "processed", "allbus_mini_clean.dta"))
bip_clean <- read_csv(here("data", "processed", "bip_clean.csv"))
skalierung_berechnen <- function(dataset, variable) {
  scale <- max(elect_clean$afd, na.rm = TRUE) / max(abs(dataset[[variable]]), na.rm = TRUE)
  return(scale)
}

title: Report
text:
4.1 BIP


Code
# scale factor for bip
skalierung_bip <- skalierung_berechnen(bip_clean, "growth_real")

# plot bip x afd polling
ggplot() +
  geom_path(
    data = elect_clean,
    aes(x = date, y = afd),
    color = "blue"
  ) +
  geom_path(
    data = bip_clean,
    aes(x = date, y = growth_real * skalierung_bip),
    color = "red"
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    name = "AfD - polling",
    sec.axis = sec_axis(~ . / skalierung_bip, name = "Real GDP growth")
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    axis.title.y = element_text(color = "blue", face = "bold"),
    axis.text.y = element_text(color = "blue"),
    axis.title.y.right = element_text(color = "red", face = "bold"),
    axis.text.y.right = element_text(color = "red")
  ) +
  labs(title = "Afd polling numbers compared to real GDP growth\n in Germany 2017 - 2026")









This plot illustrates the relationship between AfD polling and the real GDP growth in Germany from 2017 up until 2026. In the pre-COVID-19 era, both GDP growth and the AfD’s popularity had remained quite steady. However, during the pandemic, the GDP took a hit but the AfD remained steady, which indicates that the party was not able to use the pandemic-induced downturn in the economy to its advantage. The period of post-lockdown economic recovery had witnessed jump GDP whereas the support for AfD remained stagnant. When the economy began its period of stagnation, the AfD support soared, indicating an inverse connection between its popularity and economic performance.
After disclosing the negative GDP growth figures for the year 2024, the party support dropped for some time but then continued to rise. In general, the overall picture suggests that weak economic performance could trigger the growth in the AfD support during the post-pandemic times.

title: Report
text:
4.2 Unemployment


Code
# scale factor for unemployment
skalierung_unemp <- skalierung_berechnen(unemp, "unemployment_rate")

# plot unemployment rate x afd polling numbers

ggplot() +
  geom_path(
    data = elect_clean,
    aes(
      x = date,
      y = afd
    ),
    color = "blue"
  ) +
  geom_path(
    data = unemp,
    aes(
      x = date,
      y = unemployment_rate * skalierung_unemp
    ),
    color = "red"
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    name = "AfD - polling",
    sec.axis = sec_axis(~ . / skalierung_unemp, name = "Unemployment share")
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    axis.title.y = element_text(color = "blue", face = "bold"),
    axis.text.y = element_text(color = "blue"),
    axis.title.y.right = element_text(color = "red", face = "bold"),
    axis.text.y.right = element_text(color = "red")
  ) +
  labs(title = "Afd polling numbers compared to unemployment rate\n in Germany 2017 - 2026")









In this plot AfD approval rating is being compared with unemployment in Germany from 2017 until 2026. Unemployment falls before the Covid-19 pandemic. However, AfD rating is constant during that time. In the course of the pandemic, the level of unemployment rose, but the rating of AfD was quite low. Since 2022, both unemployment and AfD started increasing although the increase is much more pronounced with the AfD.
In general, it seems that the periods of unemployment rises may correspond with the upswing in the popularity of AfD, especially in the post-pandemic period. That correlation is not that pronounced, because there are likely many other factors involved.

title: Report
text:
4.3 View on the economy


Code
allbus_mini_clean_inverse <- allbus_mini_clean |>
  filter(!(ep01 %in% c(-42, -11, -9, -8, -1))) |>
  mutate(ep01 = 6 - ep01)

ep01_wght <- allbus_mini_clean_inverse |>
  filter(!(ep01 %in% c(-42, -11, -9, -8, -1))) |>
  group_by(year) |>
  summarise(ep01_mean = weighted.mean(ep01, w = wghtpew, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  filter(year > 2014)



# afd polling numbers mean per year
avg_year_afd <- elect_clean |>
  group_by(jahr = format(date, "%Y")) %>%
  summarise(
    mittelwert = mean(afd, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) |>
  mutate(jahr = as.integer(jahr))

# skalierung afd / econ satisfaction
skalierung_ep01 <- skalierung_berechnen(ep01_wght, "ep01_mean")

# plot economy satisfaction x afd polling number
ggplot() +
  geom_point(
    data = avg_year_afd,
    aes(
      x = jahr,
      y = mittelwert
    ),
    color = "blue"
  ) +
  geom_line(
    data = avg_year_afd,
    aes(
      x = jahr,
      y = mittelwert
    ),
    color = "blue"
  ) +
  geom_point(
    data = ep01_wght,
    aes(
      x = year,
      y = ep01_mean * skalierung_ep01
    ),
    color = "red"
  ) +
  geom_line(
    data = ep01_wght,
    aes(
      x = year,
      y = ep01_mean * skalierung_ep01
    ),
    color = "red"
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    name = "AfD - polling",
    sec.axis = sec_axis(~ . / skalierung_ep01, name = "Satisfaction with economy \n (1 = very bad, 3 = somewhat, 5 = very good)")
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    axis.title.y = element_text(color = "blue", face = "bold"),
    axis.text.y = element_text(color = "blue"),
    axis.title.y.right = element_text(color = "red", face = "bold"),
    axis.text.y.right = element_text(color = "red")
  ) +
  labs(title = "Afd polling numbers compared to economic satisfaction\n in Germany 2017 - 2026")









This plot compares AfD polling support with average satisfaction with the economic situation in Germany between 2018 and 2023. Overall, satisfaction with the economy decreased slightly over the observation period, falling from an average of around 4.0 in 2018 to approximately 3.0 in 2023. During the same period, AfD polling support remained relatively stable until 2022 before increasing sharply from 2023 onwards.
Consequently, the figure suggests an inverse relationship between economic satisfaction and AfD support: periods of lower satisfaction with the economy coincide with higher levels of support for the AfD. But only 3 observations are available for economic satisfaction, and the descriptive comparison alone does not establish a causal relationship.

title: The Relationship Between Economic Conditions and AfD Support in Germany
text: The rise of the AfD has sparked interest in understanding the factors that influence the support for right-wing/extreme parties. Economic reasons are often cited as key factors. This project tries to visualize the linkage between these two.

title: The Relationship Between Economic Conditions and AfD Support in Germany
text: The rise of the AfD has sparked interest in understanding the factors that influence the support for right-wing/extreme parties. Economic reasons are often cited as key factors. This project tries to visualize the linkage between these two.

title: The Relationship Between Economic Conditions and AfD Support in Germany
text:
Research Question
To what extent do economic fluctuations (measured by GDP, growth, or a decline in GDP) influence voting intention and the polling numbers of the AfD?

title: The Relationship Between Economic Conditions and AfD Support in Germany
text:
Data
We use the ALLBUS Cumulative Data Set together with official economic statistics from German federal statistical agencies. The ALLBUS dataset was chosen because it provides reliable and nationally representative survey data for Germany, covering a wide range of socio-demographic characteristics, political attitudes, and opinions on social issues. To complement these survey data, we incorporate official statistics on GDP and unemployment.

title: The Relationship Between Economic Conditions and AfD Support in Germany
text:
Results
AfD support remained relatively stable until 2022 before increasing sharply. Descriptive analyses suggest that weaker economic conditions, particularly in the post-pandemic period, were associated with higher AfD support. However, these findings are exploratory and require confirmation through regression analysis.

title: StatProg2 Group Project
text: Our analysis examines the relationship between macroeconomic conditions in Germany and support for the AfD, drawing on federal polling data, real GDP growth, unemployment figures, and ALLBUS survey data for the period from 2017 onward. Looking first at AfD polling in isolation, support followed a distinctly non-linear path. After an initial decline over the course of 2017 and a partial recovery later that year, polling entered a phase of relative stagnation between 2018 and 2020. The onset of the COVID-19 pandemic coincided with a further drop and a sustained period at lower levels. From 2022 into 2023, support then roughly doubled in a steep and continuous climb, followed by a marked decline in 2024. Since then, polling has resumed a slower but nearly uninterrupted upward trend. Setting these dynamics against real GDP growth reveals a relationship that appears to shift over time. In the pre-pandemic years, modest but steady economic growth was accompanied by broadly stable AfD support. During the early pandemic, polling and growth declined together, suggesting that the party did not benefit from the weakening economy in this phase; support likewise remained low through the post-lockdown recovery. The pattern changes from 2022 onward: as growth slowed into stagnation, AfD support rose sharply. Notably, support fell again shortly after the recessionary 2024 figures were published, before resuming its climb as the economy edged slowly out of recession. Taken together, the descriptive evidence points to a link between a weak economy and stronger AfD support that appears more pronounced in the post-COVID period than before it. We emphasise that these are exploratory observations based on the co-movement of the series; a formal statistical test is required to establish whether the association is robust once other factors are accounted for.

title: Group Reflection
text:
For each skill area, describe what your group actually used it for. If you did not use a skill, say so and note why.


What we did: We only created a function once (till now), because other repeating tasks were not suitable for functions.
What worked well: The one function we created works quite well (its a really simple one)
What would have been hard: To create a function that generates our plots. Because our plots use little to no repeating data, a function would have required a large number of arguments as input. It was faster and easier to rewrite the short section that repeated once. The other problem was that we always used different data sets for each chart, which would have required even more arguments for the function. If we had found a dataset that contained all the necessary variables, we could have written a function



What we did: We wrote a significant portion of the code together during calls, where the four of us were able to quickly resolve most errors. Since we had (and still have) widely varying levels of prior knowledge, we were able to help each other effectively within the group. Otherwise, we tried to interpret R’s error messages, using AI as a last resort to have the errors explained to us. This allowed us to fix all the errors independently without having to blindly copy code from the AI.
What worked well: Helping each other within the group
What was hard: /



What we did: We frequently created new branches so that we could all work on different aspects of the project simultaneously. Either a branch was worked on by only one person at a time, or—if multiple people were working on the same branch—we clearly communicated beforehand who was allowed to edit which file to avoid conflicts. Thanks to version control, we could always revert to an earlier state, though we haven’t needed to do so (so far). GitHub also ensured that everyone was notified whenever someone else completed a task. About halfway through the project, we adopted a workflow that worked well for everyone: we would call each other at midday to discuss what needed to be done. Afterward, tasks were assigned, and everyone worked on their respective parts, uploading their work once finished. In this way, we worked our way toward completion step by step.
What worked well: We started by coding together via a call. Later, we coordinated together, followed by individual coding. Thanks to Git, there were no version conflicts.
What was hard: Establishing our system. In the beginning, changes were sometimes made directly to the main branch; due to unclear communication and a failure to create separate branches, people would edit the same file simultaneously, leading to conflicts that could have easily been avoided.



What we did: We experimented with rendering our website and looked at early rendered outputs. This gave us feedback as to what parts of our repository structure worked and what did not.
What worked well: Editing the index in _quarto.yml to give us the desired project structure was luckily very simple and allowed us to fix the structure very quickly.
What was hard: During rendering, we did run into conflicts, notably the allbus_mini data set, but we did eventually find the issues and made it work.



What we did: After an in-group discussion, we decided not to create a project-specific R package, because our goals did not require the use of complicated and manually generated functions.
What worked well: The in-group discussion went very quickly and we came to a fast agreement.
What was hard: This week, nothing really.



What we did: After choosing the cumulative allbus data set, we quickly ran into the problem of storage. The original file was over 160MB large and by far exceeded the limit GitHub allowed us to push (100MB). After an in-group discussion, as well as talking to the tutors, we manually filtered the large data set into topics that were relevant to the project and added a reproducible code to track exactly what we cut from the original file. The other files used in this project posed different problems. After the exhausting act of data download was completed, all data sets had to be cleaned next. This too was no easy task, especially creating a helpful time variable was at times complicated to create, because some data sets had strange encodings for the time variable. Other data sets did not follow common structural rules and treated the csv file like a spread sheet with strange subcategories in the middle of the table. Once all data sets were cleaned into a clean and acceptable format, working became much easier.
What worked well: Finding Open Source data sets about the topics we wanted to cover.
What was hard: Finding acceptably structured Open source data sets about the topics we wanted to cover.



What we did: Like the individual R package, an in-group discussion lead to the conclusion that Renv was not sensible for the limited scale of our project. What we did have to to in this department is look up the licenses of the data sets we used. Some were easy to find, others were hidden under an enormous amount of layers on several websites. For future projects, we learned that license documentation should be done instantly once one decides to include a data set.
What worked well: Coming to unanimous decisions within the group.
What was hard: Finding the license for the German unemployment data covered behind a dozen windows on the website of the unemployment agency.



What we did: Assembled four cleaned data sources, the federal election polling, real GDP growth, unemployment figures, and ALLBUS survey data. Began a descriptive analysis of AfD polling dynamics and their co-movement with macroeconomic indicators, with a formal regression model planned as the inferential next step.
What worked well: Standardising all datasets to a shared date variable made it straightforward to overlay series and read off relationships.
What was hard: Arranging the plots correctly.



What we did: Built a dual-axis time-series plot overlaying AfD polling against real GDP growth, and wrote up the observed phases as a narrative findings section.
What worked well: The dual-axis plot made the shifting relationship between the economy and AfD support legible at a glance.
What was hard: Thinking process, what data was visually appealing and the process of arranging it in a understandable way.

title: Group Reflection
text:
Key analytical decisions

Decision 1: World Bank or allbus?

In the beginning, we had the option to use either the data from the World Bank, or allbus.
We decided against the World Bank and for allbus, because we liked that it was one giant data set instead of having to manually construct a data set from the World Bank. This would make documenting the raw data much easier, we thought.
Note that at this point, we had not run into the problems the allbus data set would impose later down the line.
In hindsight, choosing the allbus data set probably caused more stress than the World Bank data would have. But at least we learned how to deal with data that is simply too large to be pushed into GitHub.



Decision 2: allbus 2021 or cumulative allbus?

After deciding to go with the allbus data, we faced another decision.
Only analysing one point in time makes it hard to form conclusions about anything.
We also realized we were completely missing time-variate variables.
For this reason, we switched to the cumulative allbus data from 1980 to 2023
After choosing the data, we would run into the problem with the size of the file, but the previous data was no longer an option because we were missing a time variable.



Decision 3: expand to multiple data sets?

Realizing that only analyzing opinions without adding objective data would make the analysis between AfD-polling (by then we had agreed on what our dependent variable would be) and multiple factors weak, we decided to add the GDP and the unemployment data to the mix and strengthen our findings

We assigned tasks only as they emerged to be as flexible as possible.

alph_allbus_mini_clean <- allbus_mini_clean[, order(colnames(allbus_mini_clean))]
alph_allbus_mini_clean %>%
  # Filtering only proper values for the ep01 variable. (personal economic evaluation)
  filter(ep01 %in% c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5)) %>%
  # Filtering only the proper values for the pv01 variable. (voting intention)
  # we remove don't know, no answer, answer rejected and not eligible to vote.
  filter(pv01 %in% c(1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 42, 90, 91)) %>%
  # we create our own voting variable and make it able to compute expected turnout.
  mutate(
    voting_intention = if_else(pv01 %in% c(1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 42, 90), 1, 0),
    voting_intention = as.factor(voting_intention)
  ) %>%
  # ep01 as factor
  mutate(ep01 = as.factor(ep01)) |>
  # recoded ep01
  mutate(ep01 = recode(ep01,
    "1" = "Very good",
    "2" = "Good",
    "3" = "Medium",
    "4" = "Bad",
    "5" = "Very bad"
  )) |>
  # we remove all unnecessary variables, but keeping the weight is very important.
  select(ep01, pv01, voting_intention, wghtpew) %>%
  # We can now plot the weighted result.
  ggplot(aes(x = ep01, fill = voting_intention, weight = wghtpew)) +
  geom_bar(position = "fill") +
  # labels.
  labs(
    title = "Voting intention in Germany \nby subjective economic satisfaction",
    x = "economic satisfaction",
    y = "",
    fill = "Voting intention"
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("red2", "cyan3"), labels = c("Will not vote", "Will vote")) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(
    angle = 45,
    vjust = 1,
    hjust = 1
  ))









As we can see, people with are more negative opinion on the economic situation in Germany are more likely to announce that they would not be voting.

title: Project Proposal
text:
4 Analysis Plan

Research question


Data basis: ALLBUS 1980-2023, linking macroeconomic time series (Destatis GDP growth) covering the election year.
Descriptive: Frequency distributions of the DVs, means/SDs of the IV across election years, cross-tabulations of region × voting behavior.
Bivariate: Correlations between GDP growth and aggregated voter turnout/governing-party vote and the change compared to the previous election cycle; chi² tests for categorical control variables.
Multivariate:

Logistic regression 1: Voter turnout ~ GDP growth + control variables
Logistic regression 2: Vote for governing party ~ GDP growth + control variables


Robustness: Interaction effects (GDP × region; GDP × employment status) to test whether economic voting is context-dependent. – Interpretation: Effect sizes (odds ratios, average marginal effects) rather than mere significance tests.

text:
5 Workflow organisation

5.1 Code style
We will follow the Tidyverse Style Guide. Code formatting will be handled using the styler package, ideally configured to format code automatically on save. In addition, we will enforce consistent formatting through a GitHub Actions workflow that checks whether the code complies with the defined style guide.


5.2 Packages
As of now we will use following packages in our project:

tidyverse
here
haven
janitor
glue
readr
lubridate
withr

If we don’t actively encounter version incompatibility problems, we will probably not use package version locks as we’re assuming that package versions are generally backwards compatible.


5.3 Git workflow
The main idea behind branching is to enable a group of people to work simultaneously on the same project without interfering with each other, while also partitioning features or logically related steps to improve clarity and flexibility. This is exactly how we will use it.
We follow a feature-based branching strategy, where each step or logically related set of steps has its own branch. These branches are accessible to all team members if needed; however, to prevent conflicts, we generally restrict work on a given branch to one team member at a time.


5.4 .gitignore
What we will exclude from git is user specific data, because it is irrelevant for others and potentially private, as well as build artefacts and OS noise, as it is irrelevant to others as well.
What we will not exclude is all relevant working data, informational files, as well as environmental files.


5.5 Weights
If we need to make graphics that are supposed to be represent Germany accurately, we will use the adequate weighting variable from the data set (I.e. wghtptew from allbus). Other data sets like the polling from dawum already use their own weights and provide the weighted means in their polling numbers.
